titreManuel: HEALING FROM THE WOUNDS OF THE SOUL

lecons.html:
3 John 2, Job 10:1

In Proverbs 4:23, the Bible says: “Keep your heart with all diligence, for out of it is the wellspring of life.” If this spring is sick or polluted, the whole of life will be a disaster. That is why the author of the letter to the Hebrews says: “looking carefully lest there be any man who falls short of the grace of God, lest any root of bitterness springing up trouble you, and many be defiled by it,” (Heb 12:15). If you carry inner wounds that have not been treated and healed, you will end up being a disappointment to yourself and those close to you, just when you least expect it. It is important to know how to recognize the wounds of the soul and to be healed of them. These existential traumas have a direct effect on the way we handle our emotions, even in adulthood. They can even directly affect our personality and our behavior in completely unconscious ways.

It is estimated that every individual carries at least three wounds of the soul. One of these bruises sometimes takes precedence over the others. To cope as best we can, we try to hide these wounds from the past behind a “mask”. But while these “masks” allow us to protect ourselves, they block us in our personal fulfillment and our daily projects. The wounds of the soul hinder our freedom and our inner harmony, and they also harm our relationships with others. We must learn to heal and keep moving toward the goal of our life. If we do not heal our soul of its wounds, we risk falling into bitterness and missing our destiny. We need to take the time to question ourselves and settle our soul’s problems. The battle we run from today will come back later with greater severity. So it is better to settle it while it is still small.

First of all, let me announce the good news: you can be healed of the inner wounds you carry. And the scars this leaves on you will make you truly strong for the glory of God.

Do you know the following saying: “From now on, let no one cause me any trouble, for I bear the marks of the Lord Jesus branded on my body.”? Of course, it is not a saying. It is a verse of the Bible, coming directly from the apostle Paul (Gal 6:17). Did you know that in this verse the apostle Paul is speaking of the scars of physical wounds? But he is speaking at the same time of inner wounds. He speaks of sorrows that are those of the heart. He asks that no one cause him any more, which supposes that he had had them and was already healed. Then he speaks of the marks of Jesus Christ. “These marks of Jesus” that the apostle Paul boasts about are nothing more and nothing less than the bruises of life and ministry which, instead of bleeding, shine. These things that should have weakened him became sources of strength, because his healed heart let go of the pain, and his soul, which had developed defense systems, now uses them in the right direction and for the glory of God. These are the marks of Jesus Christ. If you are willing to let Christ turn your wounds (even and especially those caused by the Christian community) into his marks, how happy you will be! And what glory for God our Father!

Inner wounds are internal after-effects caused by one or several events that produced painful shocks. They reach the depths of our being and take away our peace of heart, and even our love for others or for ourselves, to the point of making a person’s spirit a captive. They consist of all kinds of shocks that our inner being has suffered in the conscious mind and pushed down into the subconscious, from the prenatal period until today.

So people can come into the world already wounded in their soul. I knew a girl like that in a church. She was obsessively reserved. She avoided every group. In church, she belonged to no group. She read her Bible alone, studied alone, and avoided interaction as much as she could. She hated her mother.

One day, I had a conversation with the mother that revealed the secret. She told me her story:

“She is my last child. I had already given my husband five daughters. My sixth child is a boy. When I became pregnant with this girl, I thought I was carrying yet another boy. I desperately wanted one more boy. But the ultrasound showed us it was a girl. I did not like that at all. So I began to hate the child in my womb. I said things like this: ‘What is this thing even doing in my womb? If only this thing could die! If only it could turn into blood and go away.’ That is all the wrong I admit to ever having done concerning her. When she was born, I gave her every possible care. But from her earliest age, she was already very shy and avoided me.”

Most inner wounds come from what we went through in early childhood or at conception. We even inherit them by being in contact with our parents or loved ones who are suffering. The apostle Peter speaks of the empty ways of living that we inherited from our parents (1 Pet 1:18). These wounds get worse with the shocking and traumatic events of adolescence and adulthood.

Consequences of inner wounds

  • Spirit of suicide
  • Imaginary illness
  • Fear of failure
  • Inferiority complex
  • Loneliness
  • Lack of self-confidence
  • Double personality
  • Guilt
  • Hyper-emotionality
  • Instability in the Christian life
  • Memory loss
  • Rejection of others
  • Notorious rudeness
  • Grudge-bearing spirit
  • Sexual deviation
  • Masturbation
  • Homosexuality
  • Pornography
  • Bestiality
  • Spirit of celibacy
  • Frigidity
  • Drug addiction
  • Nomadic life
  • Witchcraft
  • Depression
  • Aggressiveness
  • Demonic possession

The Bible presents several figures whose destiny was deeply affected by unhealed emotional wounds. Let us look at three particularly revealing cases.

Reuben: the fall of the firstborn

The verse that defines the turning point of Reuben’s life is this one: “While Israel lived in that land, Reuben went and lay with Bilhah, his father’s concubine, and Israel heard of it.” (Genesis 35:22)

This serious act took place in a particular family context. Reuben was born into an intense rivalry between his mother Leah and Rachel, Jacob’s favorite wife. This rivalry is clearly described in Scripture, notably when Leah names her son: “she named him Reuben. For she said, ‘Because Yahweh has looked at my affliction; for now my husband will love me.’” (Genesis 29:32)

The young Reuben therefore grew up in an environment marked by competition between the wives. A striking example is the episode of the mandrakes, where Reuben, still a child, is caught up in the negotiations between his mother and Rachel: “Reuben went in the days of wheat harvest, and found mandrakes in the field … Then Rachel said to Leah, ‘Please give me some of your son’s mandrakes.’” (Genesis 30:14)

This atmosphere of family tension probably shaped Reuben’s perception of relationships and power within the household. After Rachel’s death, it is possible that the presence of Bilhah, Rachel’s servant who had become Jacob’s concubine, appeared to Reuben as a lasting obstacle for his mother. His transgressive act could thus be interpreted as a clumsy attempt to intervene in this complex family dynamic.

The consequences of his act were disastrous. Jacob, on his deathbed, recalls this transgression: “Reuben, you are my firstborn … Boiling over like water, you shall not excel; because you went up to your father’s bed, then defiled it.” (Genesis 49:3-4)

Reuben thus lost his birthright, his blessing and his honors. His tribe gradually diminished in importance, to the point that Moses had to intercede specifically for its survival: ““Let Reuben live, and not die; Nor let his men be few.”” (Deut 33:6)

A wounded heart often has difficulty recognizing its faults and truly repenting of them. That is why it is crucial to learn to identify and heal our emotional wounds before they push us into destructive acts.

Absalom: from wound to rebellion

Absalom was the son of Maacah, daughter of Talmai, king of Geshur in Syria (2 Sam 3:3; 15:8). His story takes a dramatic turn when his sister Tamar is raped by their half-brother Amnon.

Faced with this tragedy, Absalom’s initial reaction seems measured: “Absalom her brother said to her, ‘Has Amnon your brother been with you? But now hold your peace, my sister. He is your brother. Don’t take this thing to heart.’” (2 Sam 13:20)

This apparent restraint perhaps already hides a strategy. The way he uses the word “brother” may reveal a bitter irony, suggesting that Amnon did not act as a true brother should.

Despite his advice to Tamar not to worry too much about it, Absalom himself does not forgive: “Absalom spoke to Amnon neither good nor bad; for Absalom hated Amnon, because he had forced his sister Tamar.” (2 Sam 13:22)

The situation gets worse when King David, although angry at Amnon’s act, takes no visible disciplinary action: “But when king David heard of all these things, he was very angry.” (2 Sam 13:21)

This inaction probably strengthened Absalom’s feeling that his mother’s side of the family was valued less than the other branches of the royal family. Feeling marginalized and seeing the injustice left unrepaired, his wound deepened.

After two years, Absalom arranges the murder of Amnon (2 Sam 13:23-29), then flees to his maternal grandfather. Even after his return from exile, the break with his father persists: “The king said, ‘Let him return to his own house, but let him not see my face.’” (2 Sam 14:24)

This emotional distance only made Absalom’s wounds worse, gradually pushing him toward open rebellion against his father, perhaps partly motivated by a desire for recognition and justice that he felt he had never received.

His revolt led him to a tragic end, dying without descendants to carry on his name, with only a monument as his memorial (2 Sam 18:18).

Michal: a heart gradually hardened

Michal’s story is often reduced to a single event: her contempt for David dancing before the ark and her supposed punishment by barrenness. “As Yahweh’s ark came into David’s city, Michal the daughter of Saul looked out through the window, and saw king David leaping and dancing before Yahweh; and she despised him in her heart.” (2 Sam 6:16)

But how can we understand that a woman who had once loved David deeply came to despise him? Michal’s contempt perhaps was not about worship itself, but was probably aimed at the one who had caused her so much suffering.

The biblical account reminds us that “Michal, Saul’s daughter, loved David” (1 Sam 18:20). Out of love, she even risked her life to save him from her father’s anger (1 Sam 19:11-17). Then David fled, leaving Michal behind for years.

During this separation, Saul gave Michal in marriage to another man, Palti: “Now Saul had given Michal his daughter, David’s wife, to Palti the son of Laish, who was of Gallim.” (1 Sam 25:44)

During those years, Michal probably rebuilt her life with this new husband. It is possible that they developed real affection for each other, despite the circumstances of their union.

When David became king, he claimed Michal back, not out of love but as a political symbol: “David sent messengers to Ishbosheth, Saul’s son, saying, ‘Deliver me my wife Michal, whom I was given to marry for one hundred foreskins of the Philistines.’” (2 Sam 3:14)

The pain of this new separation is plain to see: “Her husband [Palti] went with her, weeping as he went, and followed her to Bahurim.” (2 Sam 3:16)

For Michal, this forced return must have been experienced as a new wound, all the more so since David already had several wives and his claim seemed motivated more by political considerations than by real attachment. Her contempt at David’s dancing could thus be understood as the expression of a deep bitterness built up over the years.

Inner wounds do no good to anyone. It is imperative to seek healing from them, so that your heart does not harden and no longer find its pleasure in evil rather than in the Lord God.

Joseph: from betrayal to resilience

Joseph was deeply betrayed by his brothers and sold as a slave, narrowly escaping death. This family betrayal must have created in him a wound of abandonment and an immense sense of injustice. Despite the unjust imprisonment that followed, Joseph did not let bitterness invade his heart. By opening himself to God in his trials, he gradually healed from his emotional wounds, developing a remarkable capacity to forgive. This inner healing allowed him to fulfill his destiny by saving his family and Egypt from famine, turning his trauma into a source of blessing for many.

David: from childhood wounds to the scars of the soul

David’s life reveals a man marked by early psychological wounds. Neglected by his father and brothers, who did not seem to recognize his worth, David very likely developed a wound of abandonment and rejection. This suffering intensified when King Saul, whom he admired and served faithfully, tried several times to kill him out of jealousy. These traumas influenced some of David’s destructive behaviors, as can be seen in his dysfunctional family relationships and certain impulsive decisions. Yet through his psalms, we see a man who honestly pours out his pain before God, gradually finding healing and restoration. Although it came late, his healing allowed him to end his life with wisdom and to fulfill his central role in the history of Israel.

Paul: turning suffering into strength

The apostle Paul lived through a remarkable intensity of psychological suffering. Beyond physical persecution, he endured rejection by his own religious community, abandonment by his co-workers in his hardest moments, and the ingratitude of some of the churches he had founded. In his second letter to the Corinthians, he openly speaks of his moments of despair and deep anguish. Yet Paul turned these wounds into exceptional spiritual strength by opening himself completely to God: “Most gladly therefore I will rather glory in my weaknesses, that the power of Christ may rest on me.” (2 Cor 12:9). His psychological resilience, rooted in his relationship with God, allowed him to carry out a ministry of unimaginable scope despite constant obstacles.

These three biblical figures show us that psychological wounds, even deep ones, can be overcome through an authentic openness to God. Their example encourages us not to stay prisoners of our traumas, but to seek the divine healing that can turn our greatest sufferings into sources of strength and compassion for others.

lecons.titre: The four steps toward inner healing
lecons.html:
To open ourselves to divine healing, we need to follow these four steps:

  • Understand inner wounds
  • Diagnose your wounds
  • Dress the wound
  • Receive healing

1. Understand the wounds of the soul

Inner wounds can be varied, but they are classed in five categories: rejection, abandonment, humiliation, betrayal and injustice.

Rejection - Typical mask: Fleeing

Consequences of this wound of the soul

To cope with this suffering, the person will seek to protect themselves from every form of rejection by adopting certain attitudes:

  • Gets into the habit of isolating, staying on the sidelines
  • Tries to avoid the risks of emotional attachment or investment
  • Tends to devalue themselves and to be extremely critical of themselves
  • Is very perfectionist, even obsessive
  • Avoids confrontation
  • Denies certain realities and builds their own ideal world
  • Can be vulnerable to ways of escape (alcohol, drugs, sleep…)
  • Builds pessimistic scenarios and always prepares for the worst
  • Does not dare ask for help for fear of bothering others
  • Feels stress and anxiety almost daily

Abandonment - Typical mask: Dependent

Consequences of this wound of the soul

  • Continually seeks the attention of others
  • Constantly asks for help and lacks autonomy
  • Strongly fears loneliness
  • Can become hysterical, jealous, angry
  • Is afraid of the future and of having to face it alone
  • Does not accept refusals or being told no
  • Uses various stratagems to delay separations and goodbyes as long as possible

Humiliation - Typical mask: Masochist

Consequences of this wound of the soul

  • Voluntarily hurts or punishes themselves before someone else does
  • Unconsciously looks for ways to feel pain
  • Is helpful and likes to impose constraints or obligations on themselves
  • Behind a false discretion and humility hides a big ego
  • Thinks others cannot manage without their help and may put them down for it
  • Prone to hypersensitivity
  • Does not dare to have fun or take time for themselves without feeling guilty
  • Feels powerless and submissive toward those they love
  • Tends to have a very close, enmeshed relationship with the mother

Betrayal - Typical mask: Controlling

Consequences of this wound of the soul

  • Seeks to assert their personality
  • Does not hesitate to show off their strength or put their physique forward
  • Shows impatience or intolerance
  • Has difficulty managing emotions, especially anger
  • Always wants to control everything and acts like the boss to impose their wishes
  • Likes to be the center of attention
  • Has difficulty committing to people of the opposite sex
  • Blames others for their own mistakes and sufferings
  • Is particularly impressed by everything to do with fame or financial success
  • Cannot question themselves because they always believe they are right
  • Seeks to put forward their seductive assets, even to the point of manipulation

Injustice - Typical mask: Rigid

Consequences of this wound of the soul

  • Does not dare to express emotions
  • Appears cold at first sight
  • Is particularly self-reliant, but does not know how to ask for help
  • Dreads authority in all its forms
  • Shows optimism, at least on the surface
  • Cannot stay idle despite fatigue or health problems
  • Lives constantly in control and cannot let go
  • Tends to be extremely demanding of themselves, perfectionist

2. Diagnose your wounds

Answer the following questions in great detail:

  • What are your most painful moments? The hardest moments, when you suffered the most?
  • What word can define this situation, in your opinion? (Choose the closest: Betrayal, abandonment, humiliation, rejection, injustice)
  • What did you feel at the time, and what did you tell yourself?
  • What often makes you angry in life?
  • What do you feel when you disagree in a conversation with your friends, someone in your family or your colleagues?

By answering these questions honestly, you can identify your inner wounds that are still raw.

3. Dress the wound

Open the wound and clean it

The Bible says that God heals the brokenhearted and binds up their wounds (Ps 147:3). And God does everything by his word. So dressing the wound consists in examining ourselves in the light of the Word of God. Examining yourself in the light of the Word of God can cause pain at first. The Word of God is a sword. It will penetrate, touch and open the wound before letting the Balm flow. Here is how to go about it:

Get something to write with (it helps to write), and put on paper the big moments of your life that marked you negatively and painfully. Allow yourself to relive the story deeply. This lets your resentments, your fears and your pains come back to the surface. Answer the following questions: What happened? Who caused me this pain? Who contributed? Who could have helped me and did not? What was my own fault? Do I still feel guilty? Did I pray? Did God answer? If my prayer was not answered, why was that? You may not manage to answer this last question exactly. But it is important to think about it in order to bring out the hidden resentments you may have against God himself. If these resentments stay there, your faith will suffer.

Do all of the above for at least seven major events. Consider especially the events of your childhood.

Do not hold back while doing this work. Allow yourself to cry and even to pound the table. But keep doing the exercise to the end. If it starts to hurt a lot and you cannot go on, call the trainer or go to see an ABBA counseling agent.

Apply the balm

Read the following verses. This lets you realize God’s love for you. That is the Balm. If your heart can come to believe again that God loves you and values you greatly, you are healed. So you must take a notebook and write these verses out yourself, clearly, putting your name in them. Then you will spend 21 days rereading them aloud. You must read them at least once a day. But on the day you do this exercise, you will read them three times in a row:

Lam 3:19-23, 1 Cor 10:13, Ps 129:1-4, Ps 25:8, Ps 33:18, Ps 34:8, Ps 147:11, John 3:16, Ps 34:18, Ps 147:3, Ps 147:5, Isa 40:27-31, John 6:37, John 16:27, Ps 130:1-8, Ps 3:1-4, Matt 6:14, Luke 4:18, Heb 4:15, 1 John 3:5, Rom 4:25, Isa 53:5.

4. Receive healing

Make the following declaration as sincerely as you can. Read it a first time to get to know the content and become familiar with it. Then go through it again, praying sincerely. Do not hesitate to ask for help as soon as you feel the need.

Lord Jesus Christ, my Savior, you said that you came to heal the brokenhearted. Mine is in pieces. Until now I have worn masks to cover up. But I no longer want to hide from you. Look (point to what you wrote during the dressing phase). Here I am with all my pains. Heal me according to your promise.

From all this, I am hurting and still suffering. But from now on I refuse to go on with this suffering. I decide to take the healing that God offers me in Jesus Christ my Savior.

Jesus Christ came to heal the brokenhearted, starting with me. Yes, me, for it is written: whoever calls on the name of the Lord will be saved. And there is no waiting line with him. I receive the healing of Jesus Christ now.

God is not unjust. God did not make a mistake. God did not ignore me. God did not abandon me. God did not reject me. God did not humiliate me. God did not disregard my prayer. I have the testimony of the Bible about God’s goodness and faithfulness. I believe this testimony. God is true, God is good, God is love. Any thoughts that belittle God are liars. I reject you in the name of Jesus Christ. God loves me. He is my Father. God acted as was fitting according to his infinite knowledge and wisdom. He is doing for me far more than I have seen, understood or imagined. Besides, God has kept me until now, alive, and firmly in faith in Christ. Without the hand of God, how could I have made it through and be here? God is good to me.

I have made mistakes too. I disobeyed God by… (name the disobediences you recognize) and many others that I cannot name. In addition I have… (Name other mistakes). That is wrong. I was naive. But now it is past. I accept God’s forgiveness in the name of Jesus Christ. I forgive myself. I have the right to make mistakes, and until Jesus Christ returns, the blood of Jesus Christ cleanses me from all iniquity. I am clean by the Word of God that I have received. The righteousness of Jesus Christ has been transferred to me. I am the righteousness of God. I am righteous in Jesus Christ. I may fall seven times, I will always rise again, leaning on the grace of my God, and I will always be the righteous one, the beloved child of God, in the name of Jesus Christ.

…… (Name those who contributed to your wound) you really hurt me. It is not right. But I now decide, with the strength God gives me, to forgive you. I forgive you in the name of Jesus Christ. (You may name the people one by one, mentioning what they did, and forgive them).

…… (Name those who refused to help although, to your knowledge, they had the means). You could have helped me, but you abandoned me. You let me down. It caused me great pain. But I forgive you with all my heart by the grace of God. (Do this one by one, as before).

Christ redeemed me from the empty ways of living that I inherited from my family line. I renounce all inherited emotional suffering. I refuse to suffer, I take healing.

My God, thank you for your faithfulness. I count on your promise to truly be done with these wounds of my soul. Thank you for the restoration of my soul, Papa. I believe that you are healing me. Yes, this healing is mine because of what Jesus Christ did on the cross and because of his bruises. I am healed now in the name of Jesus Christ! Amen!

lecons.titre: One last essential step: moving toward reconciliation
lecons.html:
Forgiving in your heart is an essential step toward freedom. But when it is possible and safe, going to the person who hurt you can be a source of even deeper healing. Our Lord Jesus Christ teaches:

“If therefore you are offering your gift at the altar, and there remember that your brother has anything against you, leave your gift there before the altar, and go your way. First be reconciled to your brother …” (Matt 5:23-24)

You are not obliged to resume a toxic relationship or to take an excessive risk. But if you sense that God is inviting you to write, to speak or to meet someone in order to close an old wound, do it with wisdom and prayer. A sincere reconciliation can open the floodgates of peace and let you move forward more freely on the road to healing. And if you need to be accompanied in this step, talk to your trainer or to an ABBA counseling agent.

When our wounds heal, our old masks become marks, revealing positive aspects that influence our life. This process happens naturally and, under the action of the Holy Spirit, these marks shine and bear witness to the inner transformation. The apostle Paul, by the way, speaks of the marks of Jesus Christ…

The “fleeing” person develops great resilience. They have remarkable endurance at work, and are resourceful, inventive and efficient. They react quickly to challenges and pay attention to the smallest details. Their balance between solitude and productivity lets them be both independent and fulfilled.

The “dependent” person proves skillful and determined. They know what they want and show tenacity and perseverance. Their joyful, sociable and artistic spirit gives them a natural talent for capturing attention. Gifted with a unique sensitivity, they excel at helping others and at using their intuitive gifts.

The “masochist” person is bold and adventurous. Their deep sensitivity lets them respond to their own needs as well as those of others. A true mediator and peacemaker, they know how to put people at ease. Their generosity, selflessness and dignity make them an inspiring figure. Their sense of organization and cheerfulness strengthen their ability to create harmonious environments.

The “controlling” person reassures and protects. Their charisma and talent as a communicator make them an excellent leader, able to delegate and to value others. They know how to identify and reveal the potential of others, instill confidence and manage several responsibilities at once. Their sense of humor and their ability to defuse situations make them particularly effective and appreciated.

The “rigid” person has overflowing energy and a great capacity for work. Their enthusiasm and creativity feed their drive to act. They combine order and precision with an ability to simplify and explain things clearly. Faced with difficult situations, they know how to react calmly and efficiently.

So the marks left by our old masks become testimonies of strength and transformation. By divine action, they are no longer stigmas of suffering, but imprints of resilience and growth.

Without inner calm, we cannot have inner strength. Without inner strength, it is pointless to try to live practically according to the Word of God. Without inner strength, despite all your good will, you cannot succeed. The inner strength of the child of God comes from his God through the joy of the Holy Spirit. And God also asks us to be calm inside. “For thus said the Lord Yahweh, the Holy One of Israel, ‘You will be saved in returning and rest. Your strength will be in quietness and in confidence.’” (Isa 30:15)

You must recover your inner calm. You must be truly calm within yourself. But this will depend on the depth of your trust in God. The troubled soul lacks confidence in its own will and abilities, it lacks confidence in people, and above all it is afraid that God himself will let it down. If it can find in God a true friend and confidant, it will then be quiet and calm. Its relationships with others will be greatly blessed by it. It is important to find our inner calm through the spiritual resources available.

Here are some hidden questions that a troubled soul asks itself (the verses after each question are the biblical answers):

  • Does God love me as I am? (Jer 31:3, John 3:16, Rom 5:6-9)
  • Does he accept me without reservation? (John 6:37, 1 Pet 2:9-10, Eph 2:18-20)
  • Does he really take care of me? (1 Pet 5:7, John 16:26-27)
  • Are there reasons why he would abandon me? (Heb 13:5-6)
  • Could it happen that I wake up one day and find that God is finished with me? (Isa 46:4)
  • Does God count my mistakes, so that if they reach a certain number my condemnation is irreversible and irrevocable? (Rom 4:7-9, Rom 8:1)
  • With God, do I have the right to make mistakes? (Prov 24:16, 1 John 2:1-2)
  • Can I put everything down on God? Can I lower my guard, trusting that God is guarding me? Does God guard me enough for me to stop having to guard myself? (1 Pet 1:3-5, Luke 12:6-7)
  • Can I really count on God for my livelihood, my protection, my health, my future, my life, my profession? (Luke 12:22-32, Phil 4:6, Jer 29:11)
  • Can I stop working on myself, trusting that God will go to the trouble for me? (Heb 7:25, 1 Thess 5:23-24, 1 Cor 1:8-9, 2 Thess 3:3)
  • Can I count on God even for the efforts I have to make? (1 Cor 10:13)
  • Will God want to bless my small efforts? (Luke 12:32)

God carries us entirely. We can rest all our weight on him.

We can be calm and quiet; God’s feelings toward us are all positive. He has no negative feeling toward us. So if we drop our eggs to run into his arms, he will hold us in his arms while making sure we find our eggs again in good condition, in full number, and even more.

All things are permitted for me. I am resolved not to be enslaved by anything. But I do not have to be afraid of what may want to enslave me. It cannot enslave me if God refuses it, and God will not let anything take me out of his hand.

You can be naked before God. And if you feel like covering yourself to tease him, you can do that too; God will laugh heartily. And besides, God does not spend his time spying on us. Even though he knows and sees everything, he prefers not to look, so that we talk with him in our own terms and feelings. God loves us so much that he respects our privacy. He will knock at the door before entering your home or your heart. That is love. He is so interested in you that at your slightest word, God pricks up his ears.

On the other hand, you do not have to be afraid of God. God is indeed terrifying. He is awesome. He is Almighty and sovereign. He does what he wants without anyone questioning him. If he kills, no one will take him to court. But you are princes and princesses in God’s court. He is the King. You are not his subjects, you are his children. The restrictions on entering the King’s presence do not concern you. You can enter the presence of the King your Father at any time without being announced. The subjects will hurry to announce you and make way and room for you.

The son is always welcome at home. Even if the prodigal son, after his return, did the same foolish thing again, he would still be well received when he came back.

God loves his children. God is love. “Yahweh takes pleasure in those who fear him, in those who hope in his loving kindness.” (Ps 147:11). You cannot separate God from your care. You cannot take a single step without him. He will come with you. His heart is moved for you like that of a woman for her child. And God is more attentive than any human mother (Isa 49:15). A human mother may lack resources and strength to care for her child, but not God.

For a mother, her child remains her child no matter how many things can be held against him. If the mother of a bandit condemned to death happens to pass by the place of his execution, that execution will be hard. If everything depended on her own strength, you would either forgive the child or put them to death together. Can you glimpse a little why Jesus Christ died on the cross for us? “For the love of Christ constrains us; because we judge thus, that one died for all, therefore all died.” (2 Cor 5:14) We were condemned, and he took our place at the execution. He died to take us out of death (in all its forms) by rising from the dead.

You cannot separate God from you. You are his child in Jesus Christ (Gal 3:26), and he does not want to lose you for anything in the world. Moreover, nothing opposes his will.

titre: M2 — Healing from the Wounds of the Soul
objectifs: You know and can name your main wound among the 5 wounds of the soul.
You have begun the process of opening up to God — not just intellectually, but emotionally.
You understand that your wounds are not your destiny — they can become scars that shine.
You have dressed the wound in private: you wrote down your 7 events in detail and examined yourself before God.
You have made the Inner Healing Declaration all the way through, including forgiveness.
You have identified the people to forgive and have begun to do so.

qcm.q: According to Proverbs 4:23, why should we keep our heart more than anything else?
c: Because the wellspring of life flows from it
Because it protects us from others
Because God looks only at the heart
qcm.e: “Keep your heart with all diligence, for out of it is the wellspring of life.” If the source is sick, the whole of life suffers.

qcm.q: How many wounds of the soul does each person carry at least, according to the manual?
qcm.e: It is estimated that every individual carries at least three wounds of the soul.

qcm.q: What do “the marks of Jesus” that Paul speaks of in Galatians 6:17 represent?
c: Wounds that have healed and become sources of strength
qcm.e: The bruises of life and ministry that, instead of bleeding, shine.

qcm.q: What are the five wounds of the soul presented in the module?
qcm.e: Rejection, abandonment, humiliation, betrayal and injustice.

qcm.q: Which mask corresponds to the wound of rejection?
qcm.e: Rejection: the Fleeing mask. Abandonment: the Dependent mask. Humiliation: the Masochist mask. Betrayal: the Controlling mask. Injustice: the Rigid mask.

qcm.q: Which mask corresponds to the wound of injustice?
qcm.e: Injustice produces the Rigid mask: cold, perfectionist, always in control.

qcm.q: What lesson do we learn from the story of Reuben?
c: A wounded, unhealed heart pushes us toward destructive acts that ruin our destiny
We should avoid talking about the past
qcm.e: Reuben, wounded by the rivalry between his mother and Rachel, lost his birthright.

qcm.q: What fed Absalom’s wound after the rape of his sister Tamar?
c: He never knew what had happened
He did not forgive Amnon, and David took no action against him
He lost his faith because of an unanswered prayer
qcm.e: 2 Samuel 13:21-22: David was very angry but did nothing; Absalom hated Amnon. The unrepaired injustice deepened the wound.

qcm.q: How did Joseph overcome his brothers’ betrayal?
c: By waiting for time to pass
By opening himself to God in his trials and learning to forgive
qcm.e: Joseph did not let bitterness invade his heart: he opened himself to God and forgave.

qcm.q: What are the four steps toward inner healing?
c: Understand, diagnose, dress the wound, receive healing
qcm.e: Understand your wounds, diagnose them, dress the wound, then receive healing.

qcm.q: For the dressing exercise, about how many major events should you write down at least?
qcm.e: At least seven major events, considering especially those of childhood.

qcm.q: What does Psalm 147:3 say about God?
c: He asks us to hide our pain
He heals the brokenhearted and binds up their wounds
He pushes away those who weep
qcm.e: Dressing the wound means examining ourselves in the light of the Word of God, which heals.

qcm.q: What does the manual say about going to the person who hurt us?
c: It is required in every case
We can do it when it is possible and safe, without being obliged to resume a toxic relationship
We must first wait for them to apologize
qcm.e: Matthew 5:23-24: be reconciled with wisdom and prayer, with the trainer’s help if necessary.

qcm.q: What happens to the old masks when the wound is healed?
c: They become marks: positive qualities, like the resilience of the “fleeing” person
They stay the same but we hide them better
qcm.e: When our wounds heal, our masks become marks that shine under the action of the Holy Spirit.

qcm.q: According to Isaiah 30:15, where is the strength of the child of God found?
c: In the strength of his will
qcm.e: Without inner calm, there is no inner strength: it comes from God, through the joy of the Holy Spirit.

interpretation: 0 to 5 points: this wound is barely present in your life.
6 to 10 points: this wound is moderately present and may show up in certain situations.
11 to 15 points: this wound is significant and regularly influences your behavior.
16 to 21 points: this wound is predominant and strongly shapes the way you are and act.
champs.note: The wound with the highest score is your primary wound. If several high scores are close, you probably wear several masks depending on the context.

exercices.consigne: This is the first step of dressing the wound. It may be difficult, and that is normal. Briefly note each event and the wound felt. You will develop them in private in Assignment 1. If you need help, call your trainer or an ABBA counseling agent.

This assignment requires vulnerability, and that is intentional: healing begins with honesty. In a personal notebook (not here), develop each of the 7 events by answering these 5 questions: 1) What exactly happened? 2) Who caused me this pain? Who could have helped and did not? 3) What did I feel at the time? What did I tell myself? 4) Did I pray? Did God answer? If not, why do I think so? 5) What was my own fault? You may cry or get angry: that is the wound opening. Keep going to the end. If it is too hard, call your trainer. This journal stays private.

champs.label: I have developed my 7 events in my personal notebook.

exercices.consigne: Find a quiet place where you are alone, on your knees or in a prayer position. 1) Ask the Holy Spirit to guide you. 2) Read aloud before God what you wrote about your 7 events. 3) Tell God exactly what you were feeling, without embellishing or softening it. 4) Let the emotions come: tears are good, and anger expressed to God is allowed. 5) Identify your share of responsibility in each situation and confess it. 6) Then stay silent before God for a few minutes.

champs.label: I have dressed the wound in private before God.

exercices.consigne: Do it AFTER dressing the wound. Read it through first, then go back to the beginning, praying sincerely and filling in the blanks with your own details. You can do it as many times as needed.
exercices.intro_html:
Lord Jesus Christ, my Savior, you said that you came to heal the brokenhearted. Mine is in pieces.

Until now I have worn masks to cover up. But I no longer want to hide from you.

[Point to what you wrote during the dressing phase — your journal of the 7 events]

Look. Here I am with all my pains. Heal me according to your promise.

From all this, I am hurting and still suffering. But from now on I refuse to go on with this suffering. I decide to take the healing that God offers me in Jesus Christ my Savior. Jesus Christ came to heal the brokenhearted, starting with me. Yes, me, for it is written: whoever calls on the name of the Lord will be saved. And there is no waiting line with him. I receive the healing of Jesus Christ now.

God is not unjust. God did not make a mistake. God did not ignore me. God did not abandon me. God did not reject me. God did not humiliate me. God did not disregard my prayer. I have the testimony of the Bible about God’s goodness and faithfulness. I believe this testimony. God is true, God is good, God is love. Any thoughts that belittle God are liars. I reject you in the name of Jesus Christ. God loves me. He is my Father. God acted as was fitting according to his infinite knowledge and wisdom. He is doing for me far more than I have seen, understood or imagined. Besides, God has kept me until now, alive, and firmly in faith in Christ. Without the hand of God, how could I have made it through and be here? God is good to me.

[Confess here your own faults and recognizable disobedience]

I have made mistakes too. I disobeyed God by... _ and many others that I cannot name. In addition I have... _ That is wrong. I was naive. But now it is past. I accept God’s forgiveness in the name of Jesus Christ. I forgive myself.

I have the right to make mistakes, and until Jesus Christ returns, the blood of Jesus Christ cleanses me from all iniquity. I am clean by the Word of God that I have received. The righteousness of Jesus Christ has been transferred to me. I am the righteousness of God. I am righteous in Jesus Christ. I may fall seven times, I will always rise again, leaning on the grace of my God, and I will always be the righteous one, the beloved child of God, in the name of Jesus Christ.

[Now name the people who hurt you, one by one]

... _ you really hurt me. It is not right.

But I now decide, with the strength God gives me, to forgive you. I forgive you in the name of Jesus Christ.

[Name the people who could have helped and did not]

... _ you could have helped me, but you abandoned me. You let me down. It caused me great pain. But I forgive you with all my heart by the grace of God.

Christ redeemed me from the empty ways of living that I inherited from my family line. I renounce all inherited emotional suffering. I refuse to suffer, I take healing.

My God, thank you for your faithfulness. I count on your promise to truly be done with these wounds of my soul.

Thank you for the restoration of my soul, Papa. I believe that you are healing me.

Yes, this healing is mine because of what Jesus Christ did on the cross and because of his bruises.

I am healed now in the name of Jesus Christ! Amen!
